The Filter Metric is Safety-Critical:
Phantom Advantages in Group-Relative RL under Shaped Rewards

Juntao Yu ††thanks: Fudan University, Shanghai, China. ORCID: 0009-0002-6878-7930. Correspondence: 2750167653@qq.com. Companion artifact: rl-filter-metric-study; public core recipe: verl-recipe PR #125.
August 10, 2026
Abstract

Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO and descendants) can discard “no-contrast” rollout groups through dynamic sampling, while practical implementations expose a configurable filter metric. We identify and quantify a metric–predicate mismatch under composite shaped rewards. When the filter follows the shaped training score rather than the task outcome, all-fail groups retain nonzero within-group spread and pass the predicate; standard-deviation normalization then promotes shaping differences among failures to full-size phantom advantages. In a controlled three-arm comparison on GSM8K (Qwen2.5-1.5B, LoRA), no filtering and shaped-score filtering end at EM 0.080±0.1120.080\pm 0.112 and 0.040±0.0080.040\pm 0.008, whereas binary-outcome filtering holds 0.754±0.0050.754\pm 0.005 across four runs per arm (three default-seed reruns and one seed-123 run; mean ±\pm sample SD). On verl’s native recipe/dapo trainer, holding model, data, reward and trainer fixed and changing only the metric, the score arm requires no batch refill in any of 40 observed steps and ends at EM 0.1600.160; the accuracy arm refills in 29/40 steps and ends at 0.7630.763. Both use the same custom shaped-reward hook; neither modifies trainer or filtering code. Prior work has established shaping-induced amplification and all-fail filtering; our contribution isolates the metric–predicate semantic mismatch and directly instruments native deletion/refill telemetry. Across the tested positive coefficients λ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5}\lambda\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}, the unsafe arms collapse, while reversed-length and format probes do not collapse within 40 steps. Exploratory one-run cells reproduce the failure on MATH at 1.5B/7B and under GSPO; disabling standard-deviation normalization (Dr. GRPO) avoids the observed collapse at both scales. The practical implication is simple: filtering under a composite reward should use a task-outcome signal whose semantics are independent of the shaping term.

1 Introduction

Critic-free group-relative estimators normalize rewards within a group of rollouts sharing a prompt, Ai=(ri−mean⁡(r))/(std⁡(r)+ϵ)A_{i}=(r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(r))/(\mathrm{std}(r)+\epsilon). With a binary reward, an all-same group has std=0\mathrm{std}=0 and advantage exactly 00; DAPO’s dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025) discards such groups, and its published criterion is accuracy-based. The verl implementation (Sheng et al., 2024; verl community, 2026a) generalizes this to “drop groups whose configurable filter_groups.metric is all-same.” The published and documented DAPO recipes use metric=acc. Documented alternatives include score and seq_reward; their semantics depend on the reward manager. In our hook, score stores the composite shaped score.

This paper measures what that field is worth. Our contributions:

  1. 1.

    a controlled measurement of the metric–predicate mismatch under a shaped reward (0.0400.040 versus 0.7540.754 EM for shaped-score versus outcome filtering);

  2. 2.

    a native-trainer control-flow measurement: switching only the metric changes whether the physical refill loop is exercised (0/40 versus 29/40 steps) and changes EM from 0.1600.160 to 0.7630.763;

  3. 3.

    boundary probes across coefficient, shaping direction, model/task scale and estimator, with replication levels stated explicitly; and

  4. 4.

    a conditional negative result: re-zeroing binary-reward dead groups is gradient-redundant, whereas physical deletion and refill can still change the sampled prompt distribution.

This is explicitly not a defect report against DAPO: its published and official recipe uses the outcome-based arm of our comparison. We study a documented configuration surface and the semantic mismatch that appears when its metric is repurposed for a composite score.

2 Related work

Group-relative RL.

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) removes the critic by normalizing within groups and underpins R1-style reasoning training (DeepSeek-AI, 2025). DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) adds dynamic sampling: over-sample prompts and filter out those whose rollouts are all-correct or all-incorrect. GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025) moves the importance ratio and clipping to the sequence level. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) identifies an optimization bias in GRPO that inflates response length, particularly for incorrect outputs. Dr. GRPO also enters our results as a mechanism intervention because it removes standard-deviation normalization (§9).

Shaping under group normalization.

Several studies already establish the broad amplification mechanism. Pref-GRPO observes that normalization can turn minimal pointwise reward gaps into illusory advantages (Wang et al., 2025). GR3 analyzes optimization shortcuts created by additive length shaping (Li et al., 2026). ACOER shows that continuous length penalties on incorrect answers can collapse GRPO and proposes correct-only shaping (Lee et al., 2026). Most directly, the Dark Room study formalizes coefficient cancellation in all-fail groups and shows that removing standard-deviation normalization or dropping all-fail groups can prevent the collapse (Wang, 2026). We therefore do not claim to discover shaping-induced amplification, correct-only gating, or all-fail filtering. Our narrower question is implementation-level: when a DAPO implementation exposes the group-filter metric as a configurable field, can a composite shaped score change the predicate’s semantics and suppress the native deletion-and-refill control flow? We answer this with a metric-only comparison and refill telemetry.

Reward hacking and Goodhart’s law.

Optimizing an imperfect proxy can decrease true performance (Skalse et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2022). That literature largely studies learned reward models drifting from human preference; the failure here is narrower—a hand-written shaping term interacting with a group-normalizing estimator. The implementation-level twist is that outcome-degenerate groups can pass silently when the configured metric no longer represents the task outcome. Our finite-horizon probes further suggest asymmetric damage: shortcuts that erode task completion are more destructive than the completion-preserving alternatives tested.

Process rewards.

Step-level supervision can improve reasoning over outcome-only supervision (Lightman et al., 2023). Dense feedback is especially attractive when outcomes are sparse—the regime targeted by our analysis.

3 The phantom advantage

We use a shaped reward with a tunable phantom strength λ\lambda (length in characters):

r=outcome⁡(0/1)−λ⋅min⁡(len/512, 1).r=\mathrm{outcome}(0/1)-\lambda\cdot\min(\mathrm{len}/512,\ 1).

Among failures the shortest wrong answer scores best (“give up fast”). The probe is distilled from a real incident: a search agent whose answer length collapsed from ∼\sim24 to ∼\sim7 characters under a hand-tuned shaped reward. Under this reward an all-fail group has std>0\mathrm{std}>0, survives a shaped-score filter, and its normalized advantages point toward shorter failures. It carries no binary outcome contrast and here favors shorter failures. This is an instance of the amplification mechanism established in prior work (Lee et al., 2026; Wang, 2026); here it serves as a controlled probe of the filter metric and its downstream control flow.

4 Controlled design

The three arms differ only in which groups receive zero advantage. We implement the gate with a wrapper around verl’s advantage computation:

arm zeroes (advantage →0\to 0) corresponds to
no-filter nothing plain GRPO
shaped-score groups with shaped-reward std≈0\mathrm{std}\approx 0 metric = score / seq_reward
binary-outcome groups with all-same binary outcome metric = acc (official DAPO scripts)

Two design decisions matter. First, we zero advantages, not the response mask. For rows whose advantage is already zero, mask-dropping only changes the token-mean loss scale in our implementation. Our controlled A/B finds no consistent endpoint effect (§10); advantage-zeroing keeps the denominator fixed. Second, the gate reads the raw outcome, not the shaped scalar, so “barely failed” is never conflated with “passed”.

Setup.

We use Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024), LoRA r=32r{=}32 (Hu et al., 2021), five rollouts per prompt, 32 prompts per batch, lr 10−410^{-4} and 40 steps. Held-out validation uses all 1,319 GSM8K items (Cobbe et al., 2021). For MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), we sample 500 items at seed 42; filtering two overlength examples gives effective n=498n{=}498. Hardware comprises two RTX 5090 32 GB GPUs and one RTX PRO 6000 96 GB GPU.

5 Experiment 1: core GSM8K-1.5B contrast

val EM @ step 40 rep 1 rep 2 rep 3 seed 123 pooled
no-filter 0.247 0.038 0.022 0.014 0.080±0.1120.080\pm 0.112
shaped-score 0.044 0.031 0.037 0.049 0.040±0.0080.040\pm 0.008
binary-outcome 0.755 0.758 0.747 0.754 0.754±0.005\mathbf{0.754\pm 0.005}

All arms start from val@0 ≈0.715\approx 0.715. Runs 1–3 use the framework default seed and differ through rollout/scheduling nondeterminism; the fourth run sets rollout.seed = data.seed = 123. We therefore report four runs, not four distinct seeds. Telemetry: while training is healthy the shaped-score filter drops only ∼\sim2/32 degenerate groups per batch—the phantom groups sail through—while the outcome filter drops 16–24/32.

6 Experiments 2 and 3: tested doses and shaping direction

val@40 λ=0.10\lambda{=}0.10 λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30 λ=0.50\lambda{=}0.50
no-filter 0.055 0.080±0.1120.080\pm 0.112 0.000
shaped-score 0.033 0.040±0.0080.040\pm 0.008 0.021
binary-outcome 0.764 0.754±0.0050.754\pm 0.005 0.736

No positive coefficient in the tested grid avoids collapse in the unsafe arms; larger λ\lambda accelerates it. At λ=0.50\lambda{=}0.50 plain GRPO reaches EM 0.0000.000 with mean response length 1.01.0 token, consistent with exploiting the shortest-failure shortcut. The outcome filter’s mild slope (0.764→0.7360.764\to 0.736) is consistent with the residual length penalty applied to correct answers inside live groups. This three-point sweep does not establish a universal threshold or rule out a smaller finite-horizon-safe coefficient.

In a one-run probe, reversing the phantom so the longest wrong answer scores best (λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30) yields endpoints 0.736/0.746/0.7540.736/0.746/0.754 without collapse. This probe suggests greater risk when the shortcut destroys task structure: truncation deletes the answer, whereas padding leaves it intact and, in mixed groups, the +1.0+1.0 for a correct answer dwarfs the shaping term.

A second shaping family: format.

Length is not the only way to shape a reward, so we repeated the three arms with a format phantom instead: among failures, a wrong answer carrying the expected answer marker (#### ⟨\langlenumber⟩\rangle) scores 00 while one without it scores −λ-\lambda. This is not a contrived probe—format rewards are standard in RLVR pipelines. No collapse is observed in these one-run cells (endpoints 0.745/0.736/0.7690.745/0.736/0.769 for no-filter, shaped-score and binary-outcome respectively).

Taken together, the three probes sharpen the asymmetry from a statement about direction into one about structure:

phantom what the shortcut does outcome
length, short-favoring truncates the answer away very short outputs (as low as 1 token)
length, long-favoring pads an intact answer no collapse observed
format produces well-formed wrong answers no collapse observed

These probes support a finite-horizon hypothesis: shaping is most dangerous when its shortcut directly erodes task completion, whereas a completion-preserving shortcut can be less destructive. The reverse-length and format cells are n=1n{=}1, so they are boundary probes rather than evidence that either shaping family is generally safe.

7 Experiment 4: scale and difficulty

val EM @ 40, λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30 no-filter shaped-score binary-outcome
1.5B ⋅\cdot GSM8K (anchor, n=4n{=}4) 0.080±0.1120.080\pm 0.112 0.040±0.0080.040\pm 0.008 0.754±0.005\mathbf{0.754\pm 0.005}
1.5B ⋅\cdot MATH 0.000 0.000 0.524\mathbf{0.524} (+10.2+10.2 pp)
7B ⋅\cdot MATH 0.000 0.000 0.647\mathbf{0.647} (+12.3+12.3 pp)
7B ⋅\cdot GSM8K no dose—see below

Not a small-model artifact. On MATH, unsafe arms at both 1.5B and 7B reach EM 00 by step 20–30, while the outcome arms learn, gaining +10.2+10.2 and +12.3+12.3 percentage points respectively.

Dose is set by task difficulty relative to the model. A canary run on 7B⋅\cdotGSM8K measures val@0 =0.913=0.913 and 0–1 all-fail groups out of 32 per batch: the phantom has very low measured exposure in those sampled batches, so little collapse pressure is expected in that observed window. This is an exposure measurement, not proof of immunity. The practical concern is that shaping is often introduced when a task is hard for the current model—the regime with more all-fail groups.

“Removes the corpse, never the poison” replicates at scale. At the moment of death the shaped-score filter reports dead_fail = 32/32—every group all-fail with identical outputs—i.e. it reaches 32/32 after collapse has homogenized the batch. Captured once at each scale.

8 Confirmation on the official DAPO trainer

The arms above zero advantages to keep the token-mean denominator fixed. To rule out that this design choice carries the effect, we re-ran the contrast on verl’s official recipe/dapo trainer—real group deletion plus resampling to refill the batch (gen_batch_size=96, train_batch_size=32, max_num_gen_batches=10). Both arms use the same custom shaped-reward hook, but make no modification to trainer or filter implementation; only filter_groups.metric changes:

official DAPO, GSM8K-1.5B, λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30 val@0 →\to @40 mean length, first →\to last refill steps
metric = score 0.716→0.1600.716\to\mathbf{0.160} 265.6→13.7265.6\to 13.7 tokens 0 / 40
metric = acc 0.714→0.7630.714\to\mathbf{0.763} 270.8→309.7270.8\to 309.7 tokens 29 / 40

The refill counter is the sharper finding. Under metric=score, one generation batch is sufficient in all 40 steps: shaped rewards give nearly every all-fail group nonzero spread, so the first oversized batch retains enough groups and the refill path is never exercised. This does not mean that the predicate code is disabled or that no group is removed. Under metric=acc, 29 of 40 steps need a second generation batch (69 generation batches total, 1.725×1.725\times the score arm), and the policy gains +4.9+4.9 EM while its sibling loses 55.655.6. Thus a valid-looking configuration can retain many outcome-degenerate groups and leave the refill path inactive without an exception or warning.

9 Estimator intervention

If the phantom’s lethality comes from group normalization rescaling tiny within-group differences to full size, then an estimator that does not rescale should reduce that pressure. We test this by re-running the same three arms under two other estimator variants, both available as native configuration flags in verl (no estimator-code changes): GSPO (policy_loss.loss_mode=gspo with loss_agg_mode=seq-mean-token-mean) and Dr. GRPO (algorithm.norm_adv_by_std_in_grpo=false, i.e. Ai=ri−mean⁡(r)A_{i}=r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(r) without the std\mathrm{std} divisor).

val EM @ 40, GSM8K-1.5B, λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30 GRPO (anchor, n=4n{=}4) GSPO Dr. GRPO
no filtering 0.080±0.1120.080\pm 0.112 0.030 0.718
filter on shaped score 0.040±0.0080.040\pm 0.008 0.000 0.747
filter on binary outcome 0.754±0.005\mathbf{0.754\pm 0.005} 0.734 0.738
final length (tokens) 3–18 (unsafe) 1–2 (unsafe) 151–202 (all arms)

GSPO: the failure is not tied to the importance-ratio granularity.

The collapse and outcome-filtered recovery recur in these one-run cells. Notably gspo with shaped-score filtering is the fastest collapse we observed—EM 0.712→0.1530.712\to 0.153 by step 5 and 00 by step 25. Because this cell is a single run without an aggregation ablation, we do not attribute the speed difference to GSPO’s sequence-level aggregation.

Dr. GRPO avoids collapse in the tested cell.

All three one-run arms stay healthy and no length collapse occurs. The arithmetic explains why this intervention should weaken the failure. Take an all-fail group whose shaped rewards span roughly [−0.30,−0.05][-0.30,-0.05], so std≈0.09\mathrm{std}\approx 0.09. With normalization, A=(r−mean)/stdA=(r-\mathrm{mean})/\mathrm{std} spans ≈±1.4\approx\pm 1.4: full magnitude, as loud as any genuinely informative group. Without it, A=r−meanA=r-\mathrm{mean} spans ≈±0.12\approx\pm 0.12, while a mixed group (some correct, some not) still spans ≈±0.7\approx\pm 0.7—roughly six times louder. Std normalization, in other words, gives every group the same speaking volume regardless of whether it has anything to say.

The avoidance recurs at 7B on MATH.

A single-scale mechanism claim is weak, so we repeated the three-arm comparison under Dr. GRPO at a setting where standard GRPO is destructive. Under GRPO, both unsafe arms reach EM 00 (by step 20 and step 30) with final response lengths of 1–2 tokens. Under Dr. GRPO, all three arms not only survive—they learn.

val EM @ 40, MATH-7B, λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30 GRPO Dr. GRPO
no filtering 0.000 0.675
filter on shaped score 0.000 0.639
filter on binary outcome 0.647 0.665
final response length (tokens) 1–2 (unsafe arms) 288–333 (all arms)

The two cells that were total losses under GRPO land at 0.6750.675 and 0.6390.639, above their respective Dr. GRPO starting points of 0.5120.512 and 0.5200.520: removing the 1/std1/\mathrm{std} factor turns the trap configurations from catastrophic into non-collapsed learning trajectories. Nothing else changed—same shaped reward, same λ\lambda, same data, same 40 steps, same machine. Together with the 1.5B cell, this mechanism intervention implicates standard-deviation amplification as a causal contributor, but does not establish general Dr. GRPO immunity.

Two interventions targeting two ingredients.

In our tested cells, collapse is associated with (i) shaping-induced within-group spread among failures and (ii) std normalization that rescales that spread. Outcome filtering excludes the affected all-fail groups; dropping std normalization removes ingredient (ii). Either intervention avoids collapse in these cells. Dr. GRPO was proposed to correct a length bias that makes responses longer (Liu et al., 2025); here the same normalization change also weakens an explicitly shaped pressure toward shorter failures.

Caveat.

In the GSM8K estimator table, each GSPO and Dr. GRPO cell is n=1n{=}1 and the GRPO anchor is n=4n{=}4. Every MATH-7B cell in the second table is n=1n{=}1. What carries the weight is the repeated pattern: removing amplification coincides with removal of collapse at 1.5B on GSM8K and at 7B on MATH. We treat this as mechanistic evidence, not a performance ranking or universal robustness guarantee.

10 Negative results and limitations

Re-zeroing binary dead groups is gradient-redundant.

Under binary rewards, an all-same group already has centered advantage 00; explicitly setting its advantages to zero again is algebraically redundant. Mask-dropping those rows without refill additionally changes the token-mean denominator by 1/live​_​frac1/\mathrm{live\_frac}, a loss-scale change that Adam largely absorbs in our runs. A 20-step, 2-seed ×\times 2-arm controlled A/B on the airline domain of τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al., 2025) with a 7B policy shows no consistent effect in held-out mean reward (endpoints 0.5625/0.550.5625/0.55 with the gate off versus 0.4125/0.53750.4125/0.5375 with it on). A single-seed claim that “gating hurts by −0.15-0.15” disappears on the second seed. This result does not apply to DAPO-style physical deletion and refill, which changes prompt sampling and gradient variance even when deleted groups would have zero gradient.

Robustness to verifier noise.

Real binary signals come from imperfect verifiers. We flip the outcome with probability pp (deterministic per-sample hash; measured flip rate 0.1450.145 at p=0.15p{=}0.15), letting the noise flow through the entire channel—shaped score, filter signal and validation—and de-noise validation analytically via true=(obs−p)/(1−2​p)\mathrm{true}=(\mathrm{obs}-p)/(1-2p). Outcome filtering on GSM8K-1.5B, λ=0.30\lambda{=}0.30: at p=0.05p{=}0.05 the de-noised endpoint is 0.7450.745 and at p=0.15p{=}0.15 it is 0.7560.756, against a clean anchor of 0.754±0.0050.754\pm 0.005. Mechanism telemetry shows why this is nontrivial: noise breaks up all-same groups, so the filter’s final-step coverage degrades sharply (live fraction 0.22→0.50→0.690.22\to 0.50\to 0.69), i.e. the gate ends up dropping under a third of groups at p=0.15p{=}0.15, about 40% of the clean drop fraction. Yet performance holds in these one-run noise cells, suggesting margin in this setting.

Limitations.

Only the 1.5B⋅\cdotGSM8K anchor has four runs, and just one uses an explicitly different seed; off-anchor, estimator, shaping-direction and official-DAPO cells are n=1n{=}1. We test one model family, two tasks, LoRA fine-tuning, three estimator variants and two hand-written shaping families over 40 steps. The reverse-length and format probes show only that collapse was not observed in that horizon. The 7B⋅\cdotGSM8K cell is a measured absence of all-fail exposure, not proof of immunity. Noise robustness is tested only for outcome filtering at two levels. Finally, the official-DAPO comparison uses native trainer/filter code but a custom shaped-reward hook. DAPO itself uses accuracy-based filtering; we quantify a semantic risk of repurposing other documented metrics under a composite reward.

11 Practical rules

  1. 1.

    When filtering outcome-degenerate groups under a composite reward, use an outcome-semantic signal decoupled from the shaping term. If no reliable binary outcome exists, define and test the intended degeneracy predicate explicitly.

  2. 2.

    Dashboard two leading indicators: all-fail group fraction (the dose) and mean response length; in our collapse runs, length moves before validation accuracy.

  3. 3.

    Before adding shaping, measure the baseline all-fail frequency. Interpret this exposure relative to the model–task pair rather than model scale alone.

12 Reproducibility

The core GSM8K gate, launcher and no-GPU offline tests are in verl-recipe PR #125 (verl community, 2026b) (artifact commit 61dd7b6; verl commit e52747a); the earlier multi-turn environment is PR #121. The official-DAPO control used verl commit ad2e3c2. The companion artifact contains paper source, raw logs with resolved configurations, summaries and the figure script; plotted points are extracted from logs and tables cross-checked separately. The DAPO launcher was not archived, so this control is auditable from logs and shared reward code but not one-command rerunnable. Runtime: ≈\approx50 min per 40-step arm at 1.5B (RTX 5090) and ≈\approx60 min at 7B (RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, actor 53 GB + vLLM 29 GB == 82/96 GB).

Acknowledgments

Experiments ran on a single shared RTX 5090 workstation and a rented RTX PRO 6000 96 GB instance. This work builds entirely on the open-source verl / HybridFlow framework (Sheng et al., 2024) and its community recipe/dapo implementation, whose configurability made the question in this paper askable in the first place.
